question_html: As per Section 53 of the Companies Act, 2013, which of the following is correct regarding the issue of shares at a discount?

options.A: A company may freely issue shares at any discount to any class of shareholders, provided the discount does not exceed 10% of the face value
options.B: A company shall not issue shares at a discount, except sweat equity shares issued under Section 54, and (notwithstanding this) a company may issue shares at a discount to its creditors when debt is converted into shares under a statutory resolution plan or an RBI-approved debt restructuring scheme; any share issued at a discount in contravention of these provisions shall be void
options.C: Shares issued at a discount are always valid, provided the discount is disclosed in the prospectus
options.D: Section 53 permits discount-priced share issues only to promoters, without any other exception

answer_html:
B. A company shall not issue shares at a discount, except sweat equity shares issued under Section 54, and (notwithstanding this) a company may issue shares at a discount to its creditors when debt is converted into shares under a statutory resolution plan or an RBI-approved debt restructuring scheme; any share issued at a discount in contravention of these provisions shall be void

Section 53 prohibits issue of shares at a discount, except for sweat equity shares under Section 54 and, notwithstanding sub-sections (1) and (2), issue to creditors at a discount where debt is converted into shares under a statutory resolution plan or an RBI-approved debt restructuring scheme. Any contravening share issued at a discount is void.

question_html: Under Section 52 of the Companies Act, 2013, the securities premium account may be applied by a company for which of the following purposes?

question_html: Which of the following best distinguishes a 'capital reserve' from a 'revenue reserve'?

options.A: A capital reserve is always freely distributable as dividend, while a revenue reserve can never be distributed
options.B: A capital reserve does not include any amount regarded as free for distribution and can be utilised only for certain limited purposes (e.g., securities premium, capital redemption reserve), whereas a revenue reserve represents profits available for distribution to shareholders, for purposes such as financing business extension or augmenting working capital
options.C: Both capital and revenue reserves are created only from capital profits earned on the sale of fixed assets
options.D: There is no meaningful distinction between the two; the terms are used interchangeably in the Companies Act, 2013

answer_html:

A capital reserve does not include any amount regarded as free for distribution and can be utilised only for certain limited purposes (e.g., securities premium, capital redemption reserve), whereas a revenue reserve represents profits available for distribution to shareholders, for purposes such as financing business extension or augmenting working capital

Revenue reserves represent profits available for distribution to shareholders (e.g., to supplement divisible profits, finance business extension, or augment working capital). Capital reserves do not include any amount free for distribution and can be utilised only for limited purposes, such as securities premium and capital redemption reserve.

question_html: To establish the EXISTENCE of trade receivables as at the period-end, the auditor should:

options.B: Ask for a period-end accounts receivable ageing report and trace the balance as per the report to the general ledger, and check whether controls are in place to ensure invoices cannot be recorded more than once

question_html: Regarding the form of requesting confirmation from trade receivables, which of the following is correct?

question_html: Why does the chapter emphasise that cash should be checked by surprise, including sometime after the close of the year without prior notice to the entity?

options.A: Because SA 505 mandates that all cash counts must occur exactly on the balance sheet date and never before or after
options.B: Because surprise checks eliminate the need for the cashier to be present during the count
options.C: Because unless cash balances are checked by surprise, there can be no certainty that the cash produced for inspection was in fact held by the custodian, and shortage in one balance could otherwise be made good by transferring amounts from other balances
options.D: Because surprise checks are required only for entities with a turnover exceeding ₹500 crore

answer_html:

subject: Auditing and Ethics
question_html: While participating in the entity's physical inventory count to establish EXISTENCE, which of the following is an appropriate test-count procedure for the auditor?

options.A: Rely entirely on the entity's own count sheets without observing the count in progress
options.B: Perform the physical count personally without any involvement of the entity's staff, to avoid any risk of collusion
options.C: Observe that employees are adhering to the agreed plan, ensure appropriate supervision, verify that items are properly tagged with correct amounts shown, and reconcile test counts with tags and summary sheets, noting and agreeing discrepancies with client personnel
options.D: Restrict test counts only to items with the lowest unit value, since high-value items are inherently less prone to misstatement

answer_html:
C. Observe that employees are adhering to the agreed plan, ensure appropriate supervision, verify that items are properly tagged with correct amounts shown, and reconcile test counts with tags and summary sheets, noting and agreeing discrepancies with client personnel

Test counts by the auditor should include observing adherence to the count plan, appropriate supervision, proper tagging, reconciling test counts with tags and summary sheets (with discrepancies agreed with client personnel), and cut-off testing by documenting last receiving/shipping reports.

question_html: For verifying COMPLETENESS of inventories, the auditor should ensure that:

options.A: All inventory physically located on the entity's premises is included, regardless of legal ownership
options.B: Inventory held by third parties on the entity's behalf should always be excluded, since it is not in the entity's physical possession
options.C: Consignment inventory held by the entity as consignee should always be included in the entity's own inventory balance

For completeness, the auditor ensures all inventory that should have been recorded has been recognised, including inventory held by a third party on behalf of the entity, while inventory held by the entity as a consignee (on behalf of the consignor) is excluded.

question_html: To verify that the entity has valid legal ownership rights over inventories claimed to be held, which audit procedure is relevant?

options.B: Rely solely on the physical presence of goods in the entity's warehouse as conclusive proof of ownership

subject: Auditing and Ethics
question_html: As per AS 2, inventory is valued at:

options.A: Always at the original purchase cost, regardless of any subsequent decline in market value
options.B: The lower of cost and net realisable value, with the basis for valuation applied consistently year on year and any change in accounting policy adequately disclosed
options.C: Always at net realisable value, regardless of the original cost incurred
options.D: At replacement cost, without regard to either historical cost or net realisable value

answer_html:
B. The lower of cost and net realisable value, with the basis for valuation applied consistently year on year and any change in accounting policy adequately disclosed

As per AS 2 'Valuation of Inventories', inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. The valuation basis must be applied consistently year on year, and any change in accounting policy must be adequately disclosed.

question_html: As per Schedule III (Part I) to the Companies Act, 2013, inventories shall be classified as which of the following?

question_html: The cost of an item of Property, Plant and Equipment (PPE) should be recognised as an asset if, and only if:

options.A: The item has a physical existence and is expected to be used for more than one accounting period, regardless of measurability of cost
options.B: The item was acquired using borrowed funds, since only debt-financed assets qualify for PPE recognition
options.C: The Board of Directors has passed a resolution classifying the item as PPE, irrespective of probable future economic benefits
options.D: It is probable that future economic benefits associated with the item will flow to the enterprise, and the cost of the item can be measured reliably

answer_html:
D. It is probable that future economic benefits associated with the item will flow to the enterprise, and the cost of the item can be measured reliably

The cost of an item of PPE should be recognised as an asset if, and only if, it is probable that future economic benefits associated with the item will flow to the enterprise, and the cost of the item can be measured reliably.

question_html: Which of the following is NOT included as an element of cost of an item of PPE?

options.A: Costs of opening a new facility or business (such as inauguration costs), costs of introducing a new product (including advertising), and administration and other general overhead costs
options.B: Purchase price, including import duties and non-refundable purchase taxes, after deducting trade discounts and rebates

Costs of opening a new facility, introducing a new product (including advertising/promotion), conducting business in a new location or with a new class of customer (including staff training), and administration/general overhead costs are examples of costs that are NOT costs of an item of PPE.

options.C: Verify that depreciation is charged on all items of PPE (unless non-depreciable, like freehold land), assess that the depreciation method reflects the pattern of consumption of future economic benefits, and verify whether the management has performed an impairment assessment as per AS 28

question_html: To verify the EXISTENCE of an intangible asset such as software, the auditor should:

options.A: Rely solely on the vendor's invoice as conclusive proof that the software remains in active use throughout its useful life
options.B: Assume existence is established once the software licence has been renewed, regardless of actual usage
options.C: Verify whether the software is in active use by the entity, for example by examining the sale of related goods/services during the period in which the software has been used; if not in active use, deletion should be recorded with amortisation ceasing after the deletion date
options.D: Verify existence only at the time of initial acquisition, with no further testing required in subsequent years

answer_html:
C. Verify whether the software is in active use by the entity, for example by examining the sale of related goods/services during the period in which the software has been used; if not in active use, deletion should be recorded with amortisation ceasing after the deletion date

For verifying existence of an intangible asset, the auditor should verify whether it is in active use in production/supply of goods or services, rental to others, or administration - e.g., for software, verifying sale of related goods/services in which it was used; if not in active use, deletion should be recorded and amortisation ceased.

question_html: While verifying that intangible assets have been VALUED appropriately, the auditor should:

options.A: Assume intangible assets never require amortisation, since they lack physical substance and therefore do not depreciate
options.B: Verify amortisation only for goodwill, since other intangible assets are not subject to amortisation requirements

The auditor should verify that the entity has charged amortisation on all intangible assets, that the amortisation method reflects the pattern of consumption of future economic benefits, and that management has performed an impairment assessment per AS 28 - Impairment of Assets.

question_html: To establish the EXISTENCE of trade payables and other current liabilities at the period-end, the auditor should:

options.A: Check whether controls are in place to ensure that a purchase/expense invoice does not get recorded more than once, and obtain the accounts payable ageing report, tracing its balances to the general ledger and investigating reconciling items

question_html: Regarding the form of confirmation request sent to trade creditors, which is preferable?

options.A: The form showing the balance as at year-end, since this eliminates the need for the creditor to perform any independent verification
options.B: The form with no balance mentioned, wherein the trade creditor is requested to respond with the balance outstanding as per his own records

subject: Auditing and Ethics
question_html: A loan or advance, if material, is granted only if authorised by which of the following, depending on the entity's form?

options.A: Directors in the case of a company, partners in the case of a firm, and trustees in the case of a trust
options.B: The statutory auditor of the entity, since only the auditor's approval renders a loan valid
options.C: The Registrar of Companies, for all loans and advances irrespective of materiality
options.D: No authorisation is legally required for the grant of any loan or advance

answer_html:
A. Directors in the case of a company, partners in the case of a firm, and trustees in the case of a trust

A loan or advance, if material, is granted only if authorised by persons competent to advance it - directors in the case of a company, partners in the case of a firm, and trustees in the case of a trust; the auditor should inspect board minutes to confirm approval of material loans and advances.

question_html: Where loans or advances in the nature of loans are granted to promoters, directors, KMPs and related parties that are repayable on demand or without specifying any terms of repayment, Schedule III requires disclosure of:

subject: Auditing and Ethics
question_html: A provision is recognised when:

options.A: The entity merely anticipates a possible future obligation, without any past event having occurred
options.B: The Board of Directors decides, at its discretion, that a provision should be created, regardless of whether a present obligation exists
options.C: An entity has a present obligation (legal or constructive) as a result of a past event, it is probable that an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation, and a reliable estimate can be made of the amount of the obligation
options.D: The auditor recommends that a provision be created for prudence, irrespective of the probability of an outflow of resources

answer_html:
C. An entity has a present obligation (legal or constructive) as a result of a past event, it is probable that an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation, and a reliable estimate can be made of the amount of the obligation

A provision is recognised when: (i) an entity has a present obligation (legal or constructive) as a result of a past event; (ii) it is probable that an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation; and (iii) a reliable estimate can be made of the amount of the obligation. If not met, no provision is recognised.

question_html: A 'contingent liability', as described in the chapter, is:

options.A: Any liability that is certain to be settled within the next twelve months from the balance sheet date
options.B: A liability that has already been fully provided for in the financial statements
options.C: A liability owed exclusively to related parties, as distinguished from third-party liabilities
options.D: A possible obligation arising from past events whose existence will be confirmed only by the occurrence or non-occurrence of uncertain future events not wholly within the entity's control, or a present obligation not recognised because an outflow is not probable or the amount cannot be measured reliably

A possible obligation arising from past events whose existence will be confirmed only by the occurrence or non-occurrence of uncertain future events not wholly within the entity's control, or a present obligation not recognised because an outflow is not probable or the amount cannot be measured reliably

A contingent liability is (i) a possible obligation from past events, confirmed only by the occurrence/non-occurrence of uncertain future events not wholly within the entity's control, or (ii) a present obligation not recognised because an outflow is not probable or the amount cannot be measured with sufficient reliability.

question_html: To verify that recorded sales represent goods actually shipped/services performed during the period (OCCURRENCE), the auditor should:

options.A: Rely solely on the total sales figure appearing in the trial balance, without examining any underlying invoices
options.B: Assume occurrence is established once the sales invoices are sequentially numbered, without any further testing
options.C: Check whether a single sales invoice is recorded twice or a cancelled sales invoice could also be recorded, test check invoices with their entries in the sales journal, and obtain confirmation from a few customers to ensure genuineness of transactions
options.D: Verify occurrence only for cash sales, since credit sales are inherently supported by customer confirmations

subject: Auditing and Ethics
question_html: To perform a robust sales cut-off test (COMPLETENESS), the auditor should:

options.A: Examine only invoices dated exactly on the balance sheet date, ignoring shipments made in the preceding or following week
options.B: Assume cut-off risk does not exist where the entity recognises revenue on the invoice date rather than the date risk and rewards transfer
options.C: Restrict cut-off testing to export sales only, since domestic sales carry no cut-off risk
options.D: Perform cut-off procedures to ensure revenues are recognised in the current accounting period and not tampered with towards the period end, trace from shipping documents to the sales journal, and verify credit notes issued after the accounting period

answer_html:
D. Perform cut-off procedures to ensure revenues are recognised in the current accounting period and not tampered with towards the period end, trace from shipping documents to the sales journal, and verify credit notes issued after the accounting period

Cut-off errors typically arise where revenue is recognised based on the invoice date rather than the date risk and rewards transfer. The auditor should trace shipping documents to the sales journal and verify credit notes issued after the period-end, since these can be used to reverse fictitious pre-year-end sales.

case_facts_html: Solstice Apparel Exports Ltd. sells readymade garments to retail chains on credit terms of 60 days. question_html: For the ₹40 lakh disputed balance, under the Schedule III trade receivables ageing schedule, how should this amount be classified?

options.B: As a 'Disputed Trade Receivable', further classified as considered good or considered doubtful depending on management's assessment of recoverability, and disclosed separately by ageing bucket from the due date of payment

options.D: As 'Secured, considered good', since export receivables are presumed secured by letters of credit

answer_html:
B. As a 'Disputed Trade Receivable', further classified as considered good or considered doubtful depending on management's assessment of recoverability, and disclosed separately by ageing bucket from the due date of payment

The Schedule III trade receivables ageing schedule separately classifies disputed trade receivables (considered good or doubtful) from undisputed ones; the ₹40 lakh balance, being subject to a genuine dispute over invoiced quantity, must be disclosed under the disputed category, not as undisputed.

case_facts_html: Northgate Engineering Ltd. purchased a new CNC machine during FY 2025-26 for ₹2.4 crore, incurring additional costs of ₹15 lakh towards installation and testing, and ₹8 lakh towards an inaugural function held to mark the commissioning of the machine. The machine was also mortgaged to a bank as security for a working capital facility. CA Arjun Malhotra, the engagement partner, directed the team to verify the elements of cost capitalised, the entity's title over the machine, and whether depreciation had been correctly computed. The machine was ready for use and successfully tested in November 2025 but was put into actual production only from February 2026, owing to a delay in receiving customer orders.
question_html: Of the ₹15 lakh installation/testing costs and the ₹8 lakh inauguration costs, which should be capitalised as part of the cost of the CNC machine under AS 10?

options.A: Both the ₹15 lakh and ₹8 lakh should be capitalised, since both costs were incurred in connection with commissioning the machine
options.B: Only the ₹15 lakh installation and testing costs, since these are directly attributable to bringing the asset to the condition necessary for its intended use; the ₹8 lakh inauguration costs should be expensed to the Statement of Profit and Loss
options.C: Neither amount should be capitalised, since only the original purchase price of ₹2.4 crore qualifies as cost under AS 10
options.D: Only the ₹8 lakh inauguration costs should be capitalised, since these mark the formal commencement of the asset's productive life

answer_html:
B. Only the ₹15 lakh installation and testing costs, since these are directly attributable to bringing the asset to the condition necessary for its intended use; the ₹8 lakh inauguration costs should be expensed to the Statement of Profit and Loss

Costs of testing whether an asset is functioning properly are directly attributable costs and are capitalised as part of PPE cost. Inauguration costs, being costs of opening a new facility, are specifically excluded from the cost of PPE and should be expensed to the Statement of Profit and Loss.

case_facts_html: Northgate Engineering Ltd. purchased a new CNC machine during FY 2025-26 for ₹2.4 crore, incurring additional costs of ₹15 lakh towards installation and testing, and ₹8 lakh towards an inaugural function held to mark the commissioning of the machine.
